name: Hanko
description: Hanko is an open-source authentication and user management backend, an alternative to Auth0 or Clerk. It provides passkeys, passwords, email passcodes, TOTP and security-key MFA, OAuth/OIDC and SAML single sign-on, sessions and JWTs, and web apps add the login through the Hanko Elements web components or SDKs. This script runs the Hanko backend (public and admin API) with PostgreSQL.

notes.text: Hanko is a headless authentication API, not a web app. Port 8000 is the public API that your own application's login talks to through Hanko Elements or the SDKs; opened in a browser it only shows an API status page. The self-hosted backend has no admin UI, the Hanko Console is part of the closed-source Hanko Cloud.

Before an app can use Hanko, replace the example.com placeholders in /opt/hanko_data/config.yaml: webauthn.relying_party.id is your domain, webauthn.relying_party.origins and cors.allow_origins the https:// URL of the app that embeds the login. Then run systemctl restart hanko. Hanko 3 reads the top-level cors key and ignores the server.public.cors of older upstream examples.

Passkeys only work over HTTPS on a domain name: browsers refuse WebAuthn on an IP address, and the session cookie is marked Secure. Publish port 8000 through a TLS reverse proxy (e.g. https://auth.example.com) instead of using http://<IP>:8000 directly.

Sign-up, email verification and passcode login send emails. Set email_delivery (from_address and the smtp host, port, user and password) in /opt/hanko_data/config.yaml to your mail server; until then these flows fail. Users created through the admin API with a password can still sign in.

The admin API (users, sessions, webhooks) has no authentication of its own, so it only listens on 127.0.0.1:8001, e.g. curl http://127.0.0.1:8001/users inside the container. Change server.admin.address only behind a firewall or an authenticating proxy: anyone who reaches it can create sessions for any user.
Back up secret_keys from /opt/hanko_data/config.yaml together with the database. It encrypts the JWT signing key stored in PostgreSQL, and without it Hanko can no longer issue session tokens.
